links.paragraph: Eternal Life Hospice provides physician-supported hospice care at home in Thousand Oaks, Westlake, Camarillo, Oxnard, Ventura, Simi Valley and throughout Ventura County and Los Angeles County. Our interdisciplinary team supports patients in private homes, assisted living communities, residential care settings and skilled nursing facilities.

Behind every patient is a team of hospice-experienced physicians, skilled nurses and specialist clinicians who bring specialized clinical experience directly to the patient's home. Advanced symptom management, respiratory care, wound care and medication coordination — handled with the depth of a dedicated clinical team and the calm of people who have done this work thousands of times.

Music therapy, massage, reiki, aromatherapy, pet therapy, audiology, holistic medicine, end-of-life doula support and sound bath sessions with Tibetan and crystal bowls — offered alongside the clinical care plan, at no expense to families.
Each journey is a layered soundscape — synthesized for preview and best experienced with headphones. Offered for relaxation and comfort, not as medical treatment. Visit the Sound Bath page →

Call 805.953.7273 anytime — our clinical intake team is available 24/7 for new referrals. You can also submit a referral form at eternallifehospice.com/refer. No protected health information is required on the initial form; our intake coordinator will follow up to collect physician orders and complete the admission securely. For urgent same-day admissions, calling directly is fastest.

It is a continuation of care — one that honors the fullness of a person’s life even as that life nears its close.

When a patient meets eligibility criteria under the Medicare Hospice Benefit — a prognosis of six months or less if the illness follows its typical course — the focus shifts, but the commitment to the patient does not. Choosing a hospice is one of the most important decisions a family makes. This guide walks you through it — the questions to ask, the credentials to confirm and the signs of a hospice that will care for the whole person and family.

Hospice is a benefit under Medicare and most insurance plans, and its core is the same wherever you go: a Care Team of nurses, aides, a physician, a social worker and a chaplain; the medications, equipment and supplies related to the illness; and four levels of care that flex with need.

Those four levels are routine care at home, continuous nursing during a crisis, short inpatient care for symptoms that are hard to manage at home and respite care that gives family caregivers rest. When going out grows harder, the outside can still come in. A bed turned toward the window. Fresh flowers on the sill. A recording of rain or the ocean. A few minutes on a porch when the day allows. Simple gestures that carry real comfort, grounding a patient in the world they have always known.

To come back to the earth is to feel held by something steady and ongoing. It softens fear and brings a quiet peace. Care that honors life makes room for these moments — the open window, the morning light, the garden in view — as part of comfort, not apart from it.

Medicine eases the body. A whole-person approach also tends to the mind and the spirit. The therapies gathered here are offered to ease distress and lift the quality of a day. They surround skilled medical care; they never replace it.

The decision to begin hospice often arrives quickly. The first days can feel like a lot at once. Here is the path from your first call to care settled at home, laid out plainly, so you know what comes next.

Within the first day or two, the pieces of care reach the home. Medications tied to comfort are arranged, equipment such as a hospital bed or oxygen is delivered and set up and supplies are stocked. You meet the team who will return: the nurse, the aide, a social worker and a chaplain, each with a role in the days ahead. You are given a direct number and told exactly who answers when you call.

Hospice is a benefit under Medicare and most insurance plans. Its core is the same wherever you go: a care team of nurses, aides, a physician, a social worker and a chaplain; the medications, equipment and supplies tied to the illness; and four levels of care that flex with need.

Those four levels run from routine care at home, to continuous nursing in a crisis, to short inpatient care when symptoms are hard to manage at home and respite that gives family caregivers rest. Because the benefit is defined, the real question is rarely what a hospice covers. It is how well each one delivers it.
Comfort therapies such as music, gentle massage and aromatherapy, offered to ease distress and lift quality of life.

Once hospice is elected, Medicare covers the care related to the terminal illness, with little to no cost to the family. That includes the care team of nurses, aides, a physician, a social worker and a chaplain; the medications that keep the patient comfortable; the equipment and supplies the illness calls for; and counseling and bereavement support for the family. It is care built to surround a person, not only to treat a symptom.

Pain and symptom management is the clinical core of hospice care. Our team works under physician direction to assess, treat, and continuously adjust care — so patients are not left to endure what medicine can relieve.

End-of-life discomfort is not inevitable. With the right clinical team, the right medications, and consistent assessment, most pain and distressing symptoms can be controlled. Eternal Life Hospice brings that care directly to the patient — at home, in assisted living, or in a skilled nursing facility — so comfort does not depend on leaving familiar surroundings.

The circle is wider than it first seems. There is close family and there are old friends. There are neighbors who would help if only they were asked. There is a faith community, a longtime doctor, the people met along the way. And there is the care team itself, stepping in as part of the circle rather than apart from it.

Sometimes the circle is thin. That is its own kind of hard. Hospice can help fill the gaps, with trained volunteers for company and respite, with support groups and with bereavement care that walks beside a family for thirteen months after a loss. The circle can grow, even now, even here.
How hospice volunteers bring companionship and a steady hand and howyou can join them.

So much of these days is spent waiting. Waiting is easier with company. A volunteer sits and listens. Reads a chapter aloud. Plays a little music. Keeps watch for an hour so a tired caregiver can sleep, shower or step into the sun. None of it looks dramatic. All of it matters. Families remember the person who simply showed up and stayed a while.
